messages.content: A hot-swap PSU failed on a server with redundant power. How do I replace it?

1. Confirm in the BMC/iDRAC/iLO which PSU failed and that the other one is healthy and carrying the load.
2. Check the ticket/change covers the swap and grab the exact replacement part (same wattage and model).
3. Wear an ESD strap.
4. Unplug only the failed PSU's power cord, press the release tab and slide it out.
5. Slide the new PSU in until it clicks, then reconnect the cord to the same feed.
6. Verify the PSU LED is green and the BMC shows both PSUs healthy and redundancy restored.
7. Update the ticket with old/new serial numbers.
Rack 14 is alarming for high inlet temperature. Where do I start?

1. Check the reading against neighbouring racks: one rack or a whole row?
2. Walk the cold aisle: missing blanking panels, open rack doors, tiles moved, or cables blocking airflow.
3. Look for recirculation: hot exhaust leaking back to the front through gaps.
4. Check the nearest CRAH/CRAC unit for alarms or a failed fan.
5. If it's climbing or above the site's limit, escalate to the shift lead and facilities now, don't wait.
6. Log what you found and any changes you made.
What's a good way to label cables?

Label both ends, same label on each end. Include source and destination (e.g. R14-U22-P1 to SW03-P47), use printed wrap-around labels rather than handwriting, and follow the site's naming standard so the next tech can trace it without pulling anything.
Before maintenance on a PDU, what should I check?

1. Approved MOP/change in place, with the window and rollback plan.
2. Every device in the rack is dual-corded and the other feed (A or B) is healthy.
3. The surviving feed can carry the full load: check current load against the breaker rating so you don't trip it.
4. Notify whoever owns the affected systems.
5. Follow lockout/tagout for anything you de-energise.
If any device is single-corded, stop and plan for it before you start.
Any ESD tips before I swap DIMMs?

Wear a wrist strap clipped to bare chassis metal, keep the new DIMMs in their antistatic bags until you need them, hold them by the edges, and never set components on top of the bag's outside. Power down and unplug the server unless the vendor says the memory is hot-swappable (rare).
Server won't POST after I replaced the RAM. What do I check?

1. Reseat every DIMM you touched until the latches fully close.
2. Check the slot population order in the vendor's guide: wrong slots are the usual cause.
3. Confirm the DIMMs match the supported type, speed and rank.
4. Read the BMC/system event log or front-panel error codes; they often name the failing slot.
5. Try the original DIMMs back in. If it POSTs, the new part or config is the problem.
6. Still dead: escalate with the error codes.
What's the difference between A and B power feeds?

They're two independent power paths, usually from separate UPS/PDU chains. Dual-corded equipment plugs one PSU into each, so losing either feed doesn't take the device down. That only works if each feed can carry the whole load on its own.
Why do blanking panels matter?

They block empty U spaces so hot exhaust air can't recirculate to the front of the rack. Without them, servers suck in their own hot air, inlet temperatures rise and fans work harder. Every empty U in a cold-aisle-facing rack should be covered.
A fiber link is down. What are the basic checks?

1. Check both ends for link lights and the switch port status (admin up, errors).
2. Read the transceiver's DOM light levels if available.
3. Inspect and clean the connectors with a proper fiber cleaner; dirty ends are the most common cause.
4. Confirm matching optics (single-mode vs multimode, same wavelength) and correct TX/RX polarity.
5. Swap the patch cable, then the transceiver, one change at a time.
Never look into a fiber or optic that might be lit.
How do I write a good shift handover?

Keep it scannable: open incidents and their status, work in progress with ticket numbers, anything the next shift must do or watch (and by when), alarms that are known/accepted, and parts or access issues. Facts and ticket numbers, not stories.
A disk failed in a RAID array. What do I do?

1. Identify the exact disk from the controller or BMC, and turn on its locate LED.
2. Confirm the array is degraded but still online, and that the controller supports hot-swap.
3. Check the ticket and get an identical or approved replacement.
4. Pull only the disk with the fault/locate LED, insert the new one, and confirm the rebuild starts.
5. Monitor the rebuild; avoid touching other disks until it finishes.
Pulling the wrong disk on a degraded array can lose data, so double-check before you pull.
Can I skip the change ticket? It's a two-minute fix.

No. Small changes cause outages too, and the change process is how the site knows what was touched if something breaks. If it's urgent, ask your shift lead about the emergency change process; that's quick and keeps you covered.
I smell burning plastic in the data hall. What do I do?

Treat it as a possible fire. Follow the site's emergency procedure: alert the shift lead and security/facilities immediately (and emergency services if the procedure says so), and be ready to evacuate. Don't open panels or investigate alone. Tell responders where you smelled it.
What does N+1 mean?
You have the number of units you need (N) plus one spare. For example, if 4 cooling units carry the load, N+1 means 5 are installed so one can fail or be serviced without losing capacity.
How do I safely rack a heavy server?

Use two people or a server lift, install the rails first and check they're locked at the right U, load racks from the bottom up so they don't tip, and extend the rack's stabiliser feet before sliding anything out. Don't lift above shoulder height on your own.
What's the torque spec for the rail screws on our racks?

I don't know your rack model's spec, and it varies by vendor, so I won't guess. Check the rack or rail kit documentation or the site's standard, and use a calibrated torque driver if one is specified.
A server only has one of its two power cords plugged in. Should I just plug the second one in?

Usually yes, but check first:
1. Confirm which feed the connected cord is on (A or B) from the PDU labels.
2. Plug the second cord into the other feed, not the same one, or you get no redundancy.
3. Check that PDU has headroom for the extra load.
4. Confirm in the BMC that both PSUs show healthy and redundancy is restored.
5. Note it in a ticket. A missing cord is worth recording even if it's a quick fix.
Rack 9 has a single-corded switch and we're doing B-feed PDU maintenance tonight. Is that a problem?

Yes, flag it now. A single-corded device on the B feed goes down when that PDU is de-energized.
1. Check which feed the switch is actually on.
2. If it's on B, raise it with the change owner before the window. Options are a temporary move to A, a transfer switch, or a scheduled outage the owner signs off on.
3. Don't improvise a fix during the window. Get it into the MOP.
How full can I load a rack PDU?

Plan to keep continuous load at or below 80% of the breaker rating, and follow your site's limit if it's stricter. On an A/B pair, each side must be able to carry the whole rack alone, so keep each feed at no more than half of that if you want true redundancy. Check the PDU's live readings or DCIM before adding gear.
What's the difference between C13 and C19 power cords?

They're IEC 60320 connector types. C13/C14 is the common server cord, rated 10 A (15 A in UL ratings). C19/C20 is bigger and rated 16 A (20 A UL), used for high-power gear like GPU servers, chassis and larger switches. The PDU outlet type has to match, so check before you order cords.
How do I make sure I'm plugging into the right PDU?

1. Read the PDU label: feed (A/B), panel and circuit.
2. Match it against the rack's power plan or DCIM entry.
3. For dual-corded gear, put one cord on each feed.
4. After plugging in, check the outlet or PDU load reading to confirm it registers.
5. Label the cord at both ends.
If the labels and the docs disagree, stop and ask before you plug anything in.
A breaker on a rack PDU tripped. Can I just reset it?

Not straight away. A trip means something drew too much or faulted.
1. Tell your shift lead or facilities first.
2. Check what's on that circuit and whether a device failed or the load was too high.
3. Only reset it if your site's procedure allows it and the cause is understood. Repeated trips are a facilities problem.
4. Log it with the time, circuit and what was connected.
There's a UPS alarm going off in the electrical room. What should I do?

Don't touch the UPS controls. That's facilities' equipment.
1. Note what the display or alarm panel says.
2. Call facilities or the on-call electrical team right away.
3. Tell your shift lead.
4. Stay clear of the room unless you're asked to help and are trained for it.
5. Watch for knock-on effects on the floor, like PDUs on battery or bypass.
What's the difference between an ATS and an STS?

An ATS (automatic transfer switch) switches a load between utility and generator power. It's slower and usually sits upstream. An STS (static transfer switch) switches between two power sources, often two UPS systems, in milliseconds so IT gear doesn't notice. Both are facilities equipment, so techs don't operate them.
What's the EPO button for?

EPO is the emergency power off. It cuts power to the room or zone instantly. It's only for real emergencies, like fire or electrocution, under your site's emergency procedure. Know where they are, keep them clear, and never press one to fix an IT problem. If a cover is missing or damaged, report it.
Can I open the electrical panel to check which breaker feeds a rack?

No, not unless you're a qualified electrical worker with the right PPE and authorization. Opening panels means arc-flash and shock risk, covered by standards like NFPA 70E in the US. Check the PDU labels, the one-line diagram or DCIM instead, or ask facilities to confirm the circuit.
It's generator test day. Anything I need to do?

Mostly stay out of the way and be ready.
1. Avoid scheduled work on power or critical systems during the test window.
2. Know the test time and who to call if something drops.
3. Watch for alarms on the floor and report anything that loses power.
4. Don't touch transfer equipment. Facilities run the test.
How do I power cycle a server?

1. Confirm with the owner or ticket that a power cycle is approved. It drops whatever is running.
2. Try a graceful shutdown first, from the OS or the BMC.
3. If it's hung, use the BMC power controls. That's safer and logged.
4. Only pull cords as a last resort, and pull all of them, not just one.
5. Check it comes back and note the times in the ticket.
I need to move a server to another rack. What do I check for power?

1. Check the target rack's PDU headroom on both feeds.
2. Confirm it has the right outlet types (C13/C19) and enough free outlets.
3. Make sure the server can still be dual-corded on A and B there.
4. Update the power plan or DCIM, and label the cords.
5. Do the move under a change if your site requires one.
The PDU is showing an overload warning. What do I do?

1. Don't add anything to that PDU.
2. Check the reading and which outlets or bank are high.
3. Tell your shift lead or capacity team. Rebalancing load is a planned change, not something to do on the fly.
4. If it's climbing toward the breaker limit, treat it as urgent and escalate now.
5. Log the reading and the time.
What does it mean to balance a three-phase PDU?

Spreading the load evenly across the PDU's phases or banks so no single phase carries much more than the others. Unbalanced phases can trip a breaker early and waste capacity. The PDU or DCIM shows current per phase. When you plug in new gear, use the least-loaded bank.
Can I plug a power strip into the PDU to get more outlets?
No. Daisy-chaining power strips off a PDU is a fire and overload risk, and most sites ban it. If the rack is out of outlets, raise it so the right PDU or capacity can be added properly.
A server won't power on. Where do I start?

1. Check that both cords are seated and the PDU outlets are live. Look at the PDU outlet status.
2. Look at the PSU LEDs: none, amber, or green.
3. Try the BMC. If it answers, read the event log for power faults.
4. Reseat the PSUs, one at a time if it's live hardware.
5. Still dead: collect the BMC logs and LED states and escalate to the owner or vendor.
Can I go into the battery room to check something?

Only if you're trained and authorized for it. Battery rooms carry real hazards. VRLA batteries can vent hydrogen, and lithium-ion can go into thermal runaway, plus there's high DC voltage everywhere. If you need something checked there, ask facilities.
What does 2N mean?
Fully duplicated infrastructure. Two complete, independent systems, like two UPS paths, each able to carry the whole load on its own. Lose one entirely and the other keeps everything running.
How do I work out amps from watts?
For single-phase power: amps = watts ÷ volts. A 500 W server on 208 V draws about 2.4 A. Three-phase math is different, so use the PDU's per-phase readings or ask facilities for those.
Before I replace a PSU, how do I know it's really the PSU and not the feed?

1. Check the PDU outlet the PSU is plugged into. Is it live and showing load?
2. Move that cord to a known-good outlet on the same feed and see if the PSU recovers.
3. Check the BMC for the PSU status and its error codes.
4. If the outlet is fine and the PSU still faults, it's the PSU. If several PSUs on one PDU fault at once, it's the feed, so escalate to facilities.
Should I label power cords?

Yes, at both ends, with the device and the PDU outlet or feed (for example SRV-R14U22 PSU1 → PDU-A outlet 7). It makes PDU work and troubleshooting much safer, because you can see exactly what you're about to unplug.
Do I need to shut a server down before pulling a hot-swap PSU?

No, if the server has redundant PSUs and the other one is healthy and carrying the load. Check that in the BMC first. If it's the only working PSU, pulling it takes the server down, so get the owner to schedule a shutdown.
How can I limit how much power a server draws?

Most servers support power capping through the BMC (iDRAC, iLO and similar), and the exact steps depend on the vendor. It's a configuration change that can throttle performance, so only set it with the owner's approval or under a change. Check the vendor docs for that model.
A PDU's display is dead but the servers on it are still running. What's going on?

Often the PDU's management card or display has failed while the outlets still work. Don't power-cycle the PDU to find out.
1. Check outlet status from the PDU's network interface or DCIM, if it responds.
2. Confirm the devices still show power on that feed in their BMCs.
3. Raise a ticket for the PDU controller and tell facilities or the capacity team. Until it's fixed you're blind on that PDU's load.
What inlet temperature should servers be running at?

ASHRAE's recommended range for server inlet air is 18–27°C (64–81°F). Many sites run tighter limits, so check your site's setpoints and alarm thresholds. Measure at the front of the rack, where the server takes air in, not in the hot aisle.
Can you explain hot aisle / cold aisle?

Racks face each other in alternating rows. Server fronts face a cold aisle where chilled air is supplied, and backs face a hot aisle where exhaust collects and returns to the cooling units. Keeping the two separate is the whole point. Gaps, open doors and missing blanking panels let hot air mix back in.
Where should perforated floor tiles go?

In the cold aisle, in front of racks that need the air, and only as many as the load needs. Never put them in the hot aisle. Don't move or add perf tiles on your own, because it changes airflow for the whole row. Raise it with facilities if a rack is running hot.
The top servers in a rack are hotter than the bottom ones. Why?

Usually hot exhaust recirculating over the top of the rack, or not enough cold air reaching that height.
1. Check for missing blanking panels and open gaps around the top U's.
2. Check the rack doors and containment are closed.
3. Look for cable bundles blocking airflow at the front.
4. Compare inlet temps at the top, middle and bottom.
5. If it's still hot, give facilities your readings. They may need to adjust airflow.
A new switch blows air the wrong way for our aisles. Does it matter?

Yes. Gear has to pull from the cold aisle and exhaust into the hot aisle. A switch blowing hot air out the front heats its neighbors' inlets. Many switches come with front-to-back and back-to-front fan and PSU options, so check you have the right ones for how it's mounted. If not, order the correct fan/PSU kit before it goes live.
There's a leak detection alarm under the raised floor. What do I do?

1. Treat it as urgent and tell facilities and your shift lead immediately.
2. Don't lift floor tiles near powered equipment or step into standing water.
3. Note the alarm zone and anything you can see safely.
4. Keep people away from the area until facilities clear it.
5. Watch for alarms on nearby racks.
Humidity in the hall is reading low. Is that a big deal?

It can be. Very dry air raises static discharge risk, and high humidity risks condensation. Report it to facilities with the reading and the location, and be extra careful with ESD (wrist strap, grounded mat) until it's back in range. Don't adjust the cooling or humidifier setpoints yourself.
A CRAH unit is alarming. Should I check it?

Don't open it or change its settings. That's facilities' equipment.
1. Note the alarm or display message and the unit's ID.
2. Call facilities.
3. Watch inlet temperatures on the racks it serves and report if they climb.
4. Tell your shift lead if several units alarm at once.
Someone left a containment door open. Big deal?

Yes, close it. An open containment door lets hot and cold air mix, which raises inlet temperatures for the whole aisle and makes the cooling units work harder. If it keeps getting propped open, report it so the reason gets fixed.
What are those brush panels in the floor and racks for?

They're cable cutout seals (brush grommets). They let cables through while blocking air from leaking where it shouldn't, so cold air goes to server inlets instead of escaping. Keep them in place and use them for any new cable runs.
A rack is running hot. Can I prop the door open to help it?

No. That usually makes it worse. It breaks containment and lets hot exhaust mix with the cold aisle. Look for the real cause instead: missing blanking panels, blocked airflow, wrong fan direction, or too much load. Escalate to facilities with inlet readings if it's still hot.
Where should temperature sensors be on a rack?

On the front (inlet) side, at the top, middle and bottom, since temperature changes with height. Rear sensors are fine for watching exhaust, but alarms should be based on inlet temperature. Follow your site's standard for placement.
What's PUE?
Power Usage Effectiveness: total facility energy divided by the energy used by IT equipment. 1.0 would be perfect, with no overhead for cooling and power losses. Lower is better.
Is it okay to leave cardboard boxes in the data hall?
No. Cardboard sheds dust and fibers that get pulled into servers, and it's extra fire load. Unbox in the staging area and take packaging out right away.
Can I eat or drink on the data center floor?
No. Most sites ban food and drinks on the floor because of spill and contamination risk near live equipment. Take breaks in the break area.
How do I find a specific server in the row?

1. Get the location from the ticket or DCIM: room, row, rack and U position.
2. Turn on its locate/UID LED from the BMC if you can.
3. At the rack, match the asset tag or serial number to the ticket before you touch anything.
4. If the location and the serial don't match, stop and check with the requester.
A fan failed in a server. How do I replace it?

1. Confirm which fan from the BMC or the fan LED, and that the model supports hot-swap fans.
2. Wear an ESD strap and have the right replacement ready.
3. Open the lid. Some servers allow this while running, but check the vendor guide and how long the lid can stay off.
4. Pull the failed fan by its tab and seat the new one firmly.
5. Close up and confirm in the BMC that fan speed and status are normal.
6. Record the part swap in the ticket.
A disk is showing predictive failure. Should I swap it now?

Follow your site's process. Usually it gets replaced proactively under a ticket, before it fails completely.
1. Confirm the disk in the RAID controller or BMC, and turn on its locate LED.
2. Check the array is healthy otherwise. Don't pull a disk from an already-degraded array without the owner's okay.
3. Swap it with an approved replacement and confirm the rebuild starts.
4. Keep the old disk under your site's data-handling rules. It still holds data.
How do I replace a PCIe card or NIC?

1. Get the owner's approval for downtime. PCIe cards usually aren't hot-swappable.
2. Shut down gracefully, then remove both power cords.
3. ESD strap on, open the chassis, and note which slot and riser the card is in.
4. Swap the card, using the same slot unless told otherwise, and reconnect any cables in the same ports.
5. Power on and confirm the system sees the card (BMC or OS) and the links come up.
6. Record the old and new serials.
We're installing GPU servers. What should I watch out for?

1. Weight: they're heavy, so use a lift or two people and load the rack bottom-up.
2. Power: check per-rack capacity and outlet types (often C19), with both feeds within limits.
3. Cooling: they dump a lot of heat, so confirm the rack and row can handle it.
4. Rails: use the right kit and check the rack depth fits.
5. Cabling: plan the high-speed network cables before racking, because they're hard to route later.
I've been asked to update the BMC firmware. Anything to know?

1. Do it under an approved change with the vendor's correct firmware version.
2. Read the release notes for prerequisites or update order.
3. Never interrupt power or reboot during the flash. That can brick the BMC.
4. Confirm the new version afterwards and that the BMC is reachable.
5. Record the before and after versions in the ticket.
The BMC on a server isn't reachable. What should I check?

1. Check the management network cable is in the dedicated BMC port, not a data port.
2. Check the link light on that port and the switch side.
3. Look at the BMC's IP settings from the front panel or console, if available.
4. Try a BMC reset if the vendor supports doing it without affecting the host.
5. Still down: escalate with what you checked. Don't reset it to factory defaults unless told to.
A server has an amber light and keeps beeping. What do I do?

1. Check the front-panel or LCD message.
2. Read the system event log in the BMC. It usually names the failing part.
3. Look the error code up in the vendor's documentation for that model.
4. Fix what the log points to (PSU, DIMM, fan, disk) under a ticket, or escalate with the log entries.
A server is logging correctable memory errors. Should I replace the DIMM?

Follow the vendor's and your site's threshold. A few correctable ECC errors can be fine, but a rising count on one DIMM usually means replace it.
1. Note which DIMM slot the log names.
2. Schedule the swap with the owner, since it needs downtime.
3. Replace it with an identical, approved part and confirm the errors stop.
I'm swapping a motherboard. What do people forget?

1. Record the service tag/serial and asset info. The new board may need the system identity programmed in, per the vendor's process.
2. Move CPUs, DIMMs and cards to the same positions.
3. Note the BIOS/BMC settings and firmware versions so they can be restored.
4. Expect new MAC addresses and tell the owner or network team.
5. Return the old board through RMA with its tracking info.
How does an RMA usually work?

1. Open a case with the vendor, using the serial and the diagnostic logs.
2. The vendor ships the replacement, often with a return label.
3. Swap the part under a ticket and confirm the fix.
4. Pack the failed part in the replacement's packaging and ship it back within the vendor's deadline.
5. Record the RMA and tracking numbers in the ticket.
For drives, check your site's policy first. Many keep or destroy failed drives instead of returning them.
A decommissioned server still has its drives. Can I just pull them and toss them?

No. Drives hold data and have to go through your site's sanitization process.
1. Follow the decom procedure and keep the chain of custody: log each drive's serial.
2. Drives are wiped, degaussed or physically destroyed per policy. NIST SP 800-88 defines Clear, Purge and Destroy.
3. Store them in the secure bin until they're processed. Never take drives off site.
What's the difference between wiping and destroying a drive?

Under NIST SP 800-88, Clear overwrites data so normal tools can't recover it. Purge uses stronger methods like cryptographic erase or degaussing, so even lab techniques can't. Destroy physically shreds or crushes the media. Your site's policy decides which one each drive gets, often depending on what data it held and the drive type.
Where do I find what's supposed to be in a rack?

In the rack elevation in DCIM or your site's documentation. It shows every device by U position. Check it against what's physically there before you start work. If they don't match, report it so the docs get fixed.
Do I need to update anything when I install a new server?

Yes.
1. Asset tag it if your site uses tags.
2. Update DCIM or inventory with the location (rack and U), serial, owner and power connections.
3. Label the cables and power cords.
4. Note the network ports used.
5. Attach all of it to the ticket. If inventory isn't updated, the next tech can't find the server.
Which parts can I swap while the server is running?

Typically hot-swap PSUs (when redundant), drives in hot-swap bays, and often fans. That depends on the model. CPUs, DIMMs, most PCIe cards and the motherboard need the server powered off. Always check the vendor's service guide for that model before pulling anything live.
The server keeps losing its BIOS time and settings. What's wrong?

Probably the CMOS battery (usually a coin cell) is dying.
1. Schedule downtime with the owner.
2. Shut down, remove power, ESD strap on.
3. Swap the battery for the same type.
4. Power on and re-enter the BIOS settings and time. Record them first if you can.
A server is stuck in a PXE boot loop. What do I check?

1. Check the boot order in the BIOS. It may be trying the network before the local boot drive.
2. Check that the boot drive is detected. If it's missing, that's the real fault.
3. If network boot is intended, the provisioning side may be failing, so check with the owner or build team.
4. Don't change the boot order on production servers without the owner's okay.
A server's boot drive failed. What now?

1. Confirm the failure in the BMC or controller (many servers use mirrored M.2 or BOSS-style boot cards).
2. If it's a mirrored pair, swap the failed one and confirm the mirror rebuilds.
3. If there's no mirror, the OS is gone. Get the owner's plan for reinstall or restore before swapping anything.
4. Handle the failed drive under your site's data rules.
A server is throwing CPU overheat warnings. What should I check?

1. Check the fans in the BMC. A failed fan is the usual cause.
2. Check inlet temperature for that rack position.
3. Look for blocked airflow, like missing blanking panels or cables in front of the server.
4. If parts were recently serviced, check the heatsink and its airflow shroud are seated.
5. Escalate with the readings if nothing obvious turns up.
The rail kit for a new server is missing parts. Can I make it work anyway?

Don't improvise with mismatched rails or a shelf the server wasn't meant to sit on. A dropped server is a safety and damage risk. Get the correct rail kit from spares or the vendor, and park the install until it arrives.
How do I safely remove a server from a rack?

1. Confirm the right server (serial and location) and that the owner approved the shutdown.
2. Shut it down gracefully and remove the power cords.
3. Label and disconnect the network cables, and photo or note where they went if your site allows photos.
4. Use two people or a lift for anything heavy. Slide it out on the rails and release the latches.
5. Update DCIM and inventory.
Can I take photos of equipment in the data hall?

Only if your site's policy allows it. Many sites restrict photos because of customer confidentiality. If photos are allowed for tickets, photograph only what the task needs and keep them in the ticket system, not on your personal phone.
What's a smart hands ticket?

A request from a customer or remote team for on-site physical work: reseating a cable, power cycling a server, swapping a part, checking LEDs. Do exactly what the ticket asks, confirm the device by serial and location first, and record what you did and saw. If the request is unclear or risky, ask before acting.
What should I check before closing a hardware ticket?

1. The part is replaced and the device is back to normal: no amber LEDs, healthy status in the BMC.
2. The service is up, confirmed by the requester or owner if possible.
3. The old and new serials are recorded.
4. Cables and power are back as they were, and labeled.
5. Inventory or DCIM is updated.
6. Ticket notes say what was done, so someone else could follow them.
The vendor wants diagnostic logs. How do I get them?

Most vendors have a one-shot log export from the BMC: Dell's SupportAssist/TSR, HPE's Active Health System log, and similar. The exact steps depend on the vendor and model, so check their support docs. Attach the file to the vendor case and your ticket.
A server's front LCD shows an error code I don't recognize.

Look it up in the vendor's documentation for that exact model. Codes differ between vendors and generations, so I won't guess what it means. The BMC's event log usually gives a plainer description too.
How should I store spare parts?

In their antistatic packaging, in a labeled, organized spares area, logged in inventory so stock levels are accurate. Keep used or removed parts separate from new ones and mark them clearly. Mixing them up is how failed parts end up back in servers.
Do I need an ESD strap just to reseat a cable?
Not for an external cable. For anything inside the chassis (DIMMs, cards, boards) wear one. Some sites require one for all hands-on work, so follow your site's rule.
I'm not sure the server I'm about to work on is the right one. What do I do?

Stop and verify before touching it. Match the serial or asset tag to the ticket, turn on the locate LED from the BMC if you can, and check the rack and U position against DCIM. If anything disagrees, contact the requester. Working on the wrong server is one of the most common causes of outages.
How do I clean a fiber connector properly?

1. Inspect the end face with a fiber scope first, if you have one.
2. Clean it with a one-click cleaner or lint-free fiber wipes and the right solvent. Never use your shirt or compressed air.
3. Inspect again. Repeat if it's still dirty.
4. Clean the port side too, with the matching port cleaner.
5. Cap connectors you're not using.
Never look into a fiber or port that might be lit.
What's the difference between OM3, OM4 and OS2 fiber?

OM3 and OM4 are multimode fiber, usually aqua jackets, used with short-reach optics like SR inside a room or building. OM4 carries a signal farther than OM3. OS2 is single-mode, usually a yellow jacket, used with long-reach optics like LR over kilometers. The fiber type has to match the optic: multimode optics on single-mode fiber (or the reverse) won't work properly.
What's the difference between SR and LR optics?

SR (short reach) runs over multimode fiber for short distances, for example 10G-SR at roughly 300 m on OM3 and 400 m on OM4. LR (long reach) runs over single-mode fiber, for example 10G-LR at up to 10 km. Both ends of a link need matching optics, and the fiber type must match.
LC vs MPO connectors, what's the difference?

LC is the small duplex connector, two fibers for one transmit/receive pair, common for 10G and 25G links. MPO/MTP is a multi-fiber connector (12 or more fibers in one ferrule), used for parallel optics like 40G/100G SR4 and for trunk cables between panels. They need different cleaners.
A new fiber link won't come up. Could it be polarity?

Yes, that's common. Transmit on one end has to land on receive at the other.
1. Check both ends have the right optics and link lights.
2. Check light levels (DOM). If one side sees no receive light, polarity or a dirty or broken fiber is likely.
3. Try swapping the two fibers in the duplex LC at one end. Many LC clips allow flipping polarity.
4. If it's an MPO trunk, the polarity method (A/B/C) has to match end to end, so check the cabling docs.
The optic's DOM shows low receive power. How low is too low?

It depends on that optic. Compare the reading to the transceiver's datasheet receive sensitivity, or to the warning and alarm thresholds the switch shows for it. Low but above threshold often means a dirty connector or a tight bend, so clean and inspect both ends first.
Can Cat6 run 10G?
Yes, but only over short runs, up to about 55 m in good conditions. Cat6A supports 10GBASE-T to the full 100 m. For new 10G copper runs, use Cat6A, or use DAC/fiber between racks.
DAC or AOC, which should I use?

DAC (direct attach copper) is cheap, low-power and fine for short runs within a rack or to the next one, typically a few meters. AOC (active optical cable) is lighter, thinner and reaches farther (tens of meters), but costs more. Both need to be compatible with the switch and NIC, so check the vendor's supported list.
How do I find which switch port a patch panel port goes to?

1. Check the cabling or port-mapping docs or DCIM first.
2. If it's missing, trace it physically, without unplugging, by following the labeled cable.
3. On a live link, the network team can check the switch side (MAC or LLDP info) to confirm.
4. Update the docs once you've confirmed it.
How tight can I bend fiber?

Not tight. Follow the cable spec. A common rule of thumb is no tighter than about 10× the cable's outer diameter, and more when it's under tension. Bend-insensitive fiber tolerates tighter bends. Kinks and tight zip ties cause light loss and intermittent errors.
Zip ties or velcro for cable bundles?

Velcro (hook-and-loop) straps. Zip ties are easy to overtighten, which crushes fiber and copper and causes errors, and you have to cut them to make changes. Many sites ban zip ties on fiber completely.
A switch failed and needs replacing. What's my part?

1. Physically replace it under the change or ticket, with the same model, PSUs and fan direction.
2. Label every cable before you unplug it, and put each back in the same port.
3. The network team restores the config. Don't load configs yourself unless they ask.
4. Check the link lights and confirm with the network team that the ports are up.
What console settings do I use for a switch?

9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit (8N1), no flow control is a common default. It's vendor-specific, and some gear uses 115200, so check the model's documentation. You'll also need the right cable: RJ45 console, USB-C or micro-USB depending on the device.
Someone messaged me asking to change the VLAN on a switch port. Should I?

Not without approval. Port config changes belong to the network team and go through a ticket or change. Ask them to raise it properly, or pass it to the network team. A wrong VLAN can take services down.
How can I trace a cable without unplugging it?

Follow the labels first. If there are none, use a cable tracer or toner for copper, or a visual fault locator for fiber (never look into the light). Or have the network team blink the port or read the LLDP neighbor info from the switch. Don't pull cables to see which link drops.
I accidentally unplugged the wrong cable. What should I do?

1. If you know exactly where it came from, plug it straight back into the same port.
2. Tell your shift lead and the owner or network team right away, even if it came back up. They may need to check for impact.
3. Note what happened and the times in the ticket.
Owning it quickly is much better than letting someone else find a mystery outage.
A switch port is showing CRC errors. What can I do on the physical side?

1. Clean and inspect both fiber ends, or check the copper cable for damage.
2. Reseat the optics and cable.
3. Swap the patch cable for a known-good one.
4. Swap the optic.
5. Make one change at a time and have the network team watch the counters after each.
If errors persist, the port or the far end may be faulty.
Is it safe to use a visual fault locator?
Yes, if you never look into the fiber or connector while it's on. A VFL is a visible laser. Point it away from your eyes and others' eyes, and only use it on dark (unlit) fibers, never on live links.
How should I handle MPO trunk cables?

Keep the dust caps on until you connect. Never pull on the connector or the fanout to move the cable. Respect the bend radius. Clean with an MPO-specific cleaner. They're expensive and easy to damage.
How do I do a cross-connect request?

1. Get the ticket with both ends: panel, port and cage or rack for each side.
2. Check the ports are free and the media type matches (single-mode vs multimode, connector type).
3. Run and label the cable at both ends with the ticket or circuit ID.
4. Test it if your site requires it, for example light levels or a loss test.
5. Update the cabling records and close the ticket with the details.
A link keeps flapping. What could it be?

Physical layer first:
1. Dirty or damaged fiber, or a loose connector. Clean and reseat it.
2. A failing optic. Check DOM for unstable light levels and swap it.
3. A bad patch cable. Swap it.
4. A cable that's stressed or bent where it moves.
Have the network team check logs and counters on both ends while you work, so you can tell whether a change helped.
Should I keep spare optics on site?

Yes, if your site stocks them. Keep them in their packaging with dust caps, labeled by type (SR/LR, speed, vendor coding), and tracked in inventory. A mismatched optic, wrong type or wrong vendor coding, is a common reason a link won't come up.
Where should data cables go relative to power cables?
Keep them apart and organized, typically in separate cable managers or trays. Follow your site's standards. Good separation makes changes safer and avoids interference on copper runs.
What info should a good cable label have?

Both ends of the connection, the same label at each end: source device or panel and port to destination device or panel and port (for example R14-U22-P1 → SW03-P47). Use printed labels and your site's naming format.
How do I test a new fiber run?

Follow your site's acceptance standard. Typically that's inspecting and cleaning both ends, then a light source and power meter loss test, or an OTDR for longer runs. Compare against the loss budget. Record the results with the cable ID.
What's a MOP?

A Method of Procedure: a step-by-step plan for a change, covering what will be done, in what order, who does it, how to verify it, and how to roll back if something goes wrong. Planned work on critical infrastructure is done to an approved MOP.
What's lockout/tagout and when do I need it?

Lockout/tagout (LOTO) means isolating an energy source, locking it off, and tagging it so nobody re-energizes it while someone is working. You need it whenever work requires something to be de-energized, like electrical or mechanical work, under your site's LOTO procedure and only if you're trained for it. Never remove someone else's lock or tag.
Something's broken and needs fixing right now, but there's no change approved. What do I do?

Use your site's emergency change process rather than skipping change control.
1. Tell your shift lead or on-call manager what's broken and what you want to do.
2. Get verbal approval if that's the process, and document it.
3. Do the minimum needed to restore service.
4. File the emergency change and ticket notes right after.
Am I allowed to work on the floor alone?

Check your site's policy. Many allow routine work alone but require a second person for higher-risk tasks like heavy lifts, work near electrical equipment, or anything needing LOTO. Either way, make sure someone knows where you are, and carry a phone or radio.
Someone without a badge wants to follow me through a secure door. They say they work here.

Don't let them tailgate, even if they seem legit. Politely ask them to badge in themselves, or to call security or their escort. Report it if they push. Tailgating is how unauthorized people get onto the floor.
I'm escorting a visitor. What are the rules?

Keep them with you the whole time and in the areas their access covers. Follow your site's rules on photos, devices and what they can touch, and sign them in and out. If you have to leave, hand them to another authorized escort first. Never leave them alone on the floor.
How should I lift heavy equipment?

Use a server lift if one's available. Otherwise use two people for anything heavy or awkward. Lift with your legs, keep it close, and don't twist. Most sites set a weight limit for one-person lifts, so follow it. Racking a 30+ kg server alone at shoulder height is how people get hurt.
Any tips for using a ladder in the data hall?

Use the right rolling ladder or step platform, not a chair or a crate. Check it's stable with the wheels locked, keep three points of contact, and don't overreach. Get a second person for anything heavy or high. Watch for cable trays and sprinkler heads overhead.
What do I need to know about the fire suppression system?

Most data halls use a clean-agent or gas system. Know where the alarms and abort/hold buttons are and what they do at your site. If the pre-discharge alarm sounds, leave the room immediately. Never block nozzles or detectors, and never disable or trigger the system yourself.
The fire alarm went off in the data hall. What do I do?

Follow your site's emergency plan: stop work, leave by the nearest exit, go to the assembly point, and report to whoever does the headcount. Don't stop to save equipment or finish a task. Only go back in when the fire team or security clears it.
There's water on the floor near a rack. What do I do?

1. Don't step in it or touch anything electrical nearby.
2. Alert facilities and your shift lead right away.
3. Keep others away from the area.
4. From a safe spot, note where it seems to be coming from and which racks are close.
5. Let facilities handle the cleanup and cause.
Someone got hurt on the floor. What do I do?

1. Make sure the area is safe before helping. If it's electrical, don't touch them until the power is off.
2. Call emergency services if it's serious, and alert site security and your shift lead.
3. Give first aid only if you're trained.
4. Report the incident under your site's process, including near misses.
A customer on site wants to take a failed drive home with them.

Don't hand it over unless your site's process explicitly allows it and it's documented. Drives usually follow strict chain-of-custody and sanitization rules. Check with your shift lead or the account owner, log the decision, and get the paperwork signed if release is approved.
Someone asked me to disable an alarm because it keeps going off.

Don't disable it yourself. An alarm is there for a reason, and a noisy one usually means something real or a broken sensor. Report it to the team that owns it (facilities, security or monitoring) so they can fix the cause or suppress it properly under a ticket.
Someone asked me to swap a part on a server but there's no ticket. Should I do it?

Get a ticket first. Even if it's urgent and they're senior, the ticket is how the work gets approved, tracked and traced if something goes wrong. If it's an emergency, use the emergency process and document it right after.
The ticket instructions don't make sense to me.

Ask before you act. Contact the requester or your shift lead and clarify which device, what exactly to do, and what the expected result is. Note the clarification in the ticket. Guessing on live infrastructure is how outages start.
The ticket says rack 12 U18, but the server there has a different serial. What now?

Stop. Don't touch either server.
1. Check DCIM and nearby racks for the serial in the ticket.
2. Contact the requester with what you found: the location, the serial you see, and the serial they gave.
3. Wait for confirmation before doing anything.
4. Note the mismatch so the inventory gets corrected.
How do I write good ticket notes?

Write so someone else could pick up where you left off: what you found (LEDs, errors, readings), what you did and in what order, part serials in and out, times, the result, and anything still outstanding. Facts over opinions, and no shorthand only you understand.
I think something I did caused an outage. What do I do?

Tell your shift lead and the owner immediately. Don't wait to be sure, and don't try to quietly fix it first.
1. Say exactly what you did and when.
2. Stop making further changes unless asked.
3. Help with recovery if they want you to.
4. Write it up honestly in the ticket. The goal is fixing it fast and learning from it, not blame.
Who should I escalate to when something's beyond me?

Follow your site's escalation path, usually your shift lead first, then the on-call manager or specialist team (facilities for power and cooling, network for connectivity, the owner for their systems). If it's a safety or emergency issue, go straight to emergency procedures. Escalating early is the right call.
How do I do a simple root cause analysis?

1. Write the timeline: what happened, when, and what was seen.
2. Ask "why" repeatedly, the 5 Whys, until you reach a cause you can actually fix.
3. Separate the trigger from the underlying cause.
4. List actions that prevent a repeat, each with an owner and a date.
Keep it factual and blame-free.
My change didn't go as planned. When should I roll back?

When the MOP's verification step fails or you see impact you didn't expect. Don't push on hoping it'll sort itself out.
1. Stop and tell the change owner.
2. Follow the rollback steps in the MOP.
3. Confirm the system is back to its starting state.
4. Document what happened.
What should I check before starting any work on the floor?

1. The ticket or change is approved, and you understand what's being asked.
2. You have the right device, confirmed by serial and location.
3. You have the right parts, tools and ESD gear.
4. You know the rollback or what "done" looks like.
5. The owner is aware if there's any impact.
6. Your workspace and access route are clear.
What should I wear in the data hall?

Closed-toe shoes, clothing that won't snag, and hearing protection in loud areas. Keep long hair and lanyards secured. Follow your site's rules: some require safety shoes or high-vis in certain areas, and anyone doing electrical work needs the specific PPE for it.
Our data hall is really loud. Do I need ear protection?
In many halls, yes. High-density server rooms can be loud enough to damage hearing over a long shift. Use the hearing protection your site provides, especially for long periods near the racks.
Can I lend my badge or keys to a colleague who forgot theirs?
No. Access is personal and logged under your name. Send them to security for a temporary badge. Lending a badge is usually a serious policy violation, even for a coworker.
Should I report a near miss if nobody got hurt?
Yes. Near misses are free lessons. Report it through your site's safety process with what happened and what could have happened. That's how the hazard gets fixed before someone does get hurt.
I have several tickets open. How do I prioritize?

Safety issues come first, then by priority and SLA: outages and P1s before routine work. Check with your shift lead when priorities conflict, and tell requesters if their ticket will be delayed. Don't let low-priority work quietly crowd out something urgent.
How do I tell a requester their ticket will be late?

Tell them early and be specific: what's holding it up (parts, access, approval), when you expect to do it, and whether they need to do anything. For example: "The replacement PSU arrives tomorrow morning. I'll swap it at 9:00 and update you." Then update the ticket.
How do I say no to a request that isn't safe?

Say it plainly and give the reason, then offer the safe route. For example: "I can't work on that PDU without an approved MOP and LOTO. I can raise the change now and get it scheduled." If they push, escalate to your shift lead. You're never expected to do unsafe work.
I'm starting at a new site. What should I learn first?

1. Emergency exits, assembly points, and where the EPOs and fire alarm pulls are.
2. Site safety rules and who to call for facilities, security and on-call.
3. Access rules and escort procedures.
4. How rooms, rows and racks are named, and where DCIM and runbooks live.
5. Where spares, tools and ESD gear are kept.
6. The ticket and change process.
How are rack locations usually named?

It depends on the site, but typically it's room or hall, then row, then rack number, then U position, for example DH2-R07-RK12-U22. U positions usually count from the bottom. Check your site's naming standard, and always use full locations in tickets.
I'm on a 12-hour shift. Any advice?

Take your breaks, eat, and drink water off the floor. Fatigue leads to mistakes on live gear. Leave risky work for when you're fresh or have a second person, and do a proper handover so nothing gets lost at shift change.
What's an SLA in smart hands work?

The service level agreement: how quickly a request has to be acknowledged and completed, usually depending on priority. Know the SLAs for your tickets, update the ticket as you go, and flag early if you'll miss one.
What's the part number for a replacement PSU for our servers?

I don't know your exact servers, and part numbers vary by model and configuration, so I won't guess. Look it up by the server's service tag or serial on the vendor's support site, or in your site's spares system.
What's the default root password for the BMC on these servers?

I won't help with default credentials. Production BMCs shouldn't be on factory defaults anyway. Get the credentials from your site's password vault or the system owner. If a BMC is still on its default password, report it.
What's our site's generator capacity?
I don't know your site's specifics. That's in facilities' documentation, the electrical one-line diagram, or your site's capacity records. Ask the facilities team if you can't find it.
Will this third-party optic work in our switches?

It depends on the switch vendor, model, software version, and whether it enforces optic coding. Check the vendor's compatibility matrix or ask the network team. Some switches reject or warn on non-approved optics.
How long will a RAID 6 rebuild take?

It depends on drive size, array size, controller, and how busy the server is. Anything from hours to more than a day for large drives. Watch the progress in the RAID controller or BMC rather than estimating. RAID 6 survives two drive failures, but avoid touching other drives until the rebuild finishes.
What size breaker feeds rack 12?
I can't see your site's records. Check the PDU or whip label (it usually shows the panel, circuit and rating), the one-line diagram, or DCIM. Ask facilities if the labels are missing or don't match.
Can our servers run at 35°C inlet?

It depends on the equipment. Check the vendor's spec for that model. ASHRAE's allowable classes go above the 18–27°C recommended range, but not all gear is rated for it, and your site's limits apply anyway. Treat 35°C as an issue to escalate unless the site says otherwise.
Which rack in row 4 has the most power headroom?

I don't have your live data. Check DCIM or the PDU readings for each rack on both feeds, and remember each feed has to carry the full load alone if the other fails. The capacity or facilities team can confirm before you plan an install.
A server has an amber PSU light.

1. Check the BMC: which PSU, and what's the fault (failed, lost input, mismatch)?
2. Check that PSU's power cord and the PDU outlet are live.
3. If the input is fine and the PSU reports failed, replace it under a ticket. It's hot-swap if the other PSU is healthy.
The BMC says 'lost input' and the PDU outlet looks fine.

Then it's likely the cord or the connection.
1. Reseat the cord at both ends.
2. Swap in a known-good cord.
3. Try a different outlet on the same feed.
If it still says lost input, the PSU's input stage may be bad, so replace the PSU. If several servers on that PDU show the same thing, escalate to facilities, because it could be the feed.
I need to swap a failed disk in a RAID 5 array.

1. Confirm in the controller which disk failed and that the array is degraded but online.
2. Turn on that disk's locate LED.
3. Check hot-swap is supported, and get an approved matching replacement.
4. Pull only the failed disk, insert the new one, and confirm the rebuild starts.
Why do you keep saying to double-check the disk?
Because RAID 5 only survives one failed disk. The array is already degraded, so pulling a healthy disk by mistake takes it offline and can lose data. Two seconds checking the LED is worth it.
Can you help me write a shift handover?

Sure. Give me your open tickets and anything unusual from the shift, and I'll format it. A good handover covers:
1. Open incidents and their status.
2. Work in progress with ticket numbers.
3. Anything due or to watch on the next shift.
4. Known alarms.
5. Parts or access issues.
Tickets: INC-4412 PSU swap done waiting on customer confirm, CHG-221 tonight fiber work in row 3. Also the CRAH-2 alarm was a false alarm per facilities.

Shift handover

Open:
- INC-4412: PSU replaced, waiting on customer to confirm service. Follow up if there's no reply by mid-shift.

Scheduled:
- CHG-221: fiber work in row 3 tonight. Check the MOP and parts before the window.

Alarms:
- CRAH-2 alarm: facilities confirmed it was a false alarm. No action needed, but report it if it comes back.

Nothing else outstanding.
What's the difference between N+1 and 2N?
N+1 is what you need (N) plus one spare unit. 2N is two complete, independent systems, each able to carry the full load alone. 2N survives losing an entire side. N+1 survives losing one unit.
Which one is our site?

I don't know your site's design. It's in the facilities or design documentation, and it can differ by system: power might be 2N while cooling is N+1. Ask facilities if it isn't documented where you can see it.
I need to rack a 2U server in rack 7.

1. Check the rack elevation for a free 2U slot, and that the power and network plan cover it.
2. Install the rails at the right U and check they're level and locked.
3. Lift with two people or a lift and slide it in until the latches click.
4. Dual-cord it to the A and B feeds, and label the cords and cables.
5. Update DCIM and the ticket.
The only free space is at the very top. Is that okay?

It can be, but check two things first. Is it light enough to lift that high safely? Use the lift or two people, never solo at head height. And does the top of the rack get enough cooling? Inlet temps are often highest up there. If it's a heavy or hot server, raise it with your lead. They may prefer to rearrange the rack.
